questions.title: How can the Ninth Circuit issue a stay pending appeal before releasing its full merits opinion?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The panel says the case is "submitted for decision" and that "an opinion on the merits will issue in due course," but in the meantime it vacates its prior stays and enters a new stay pending appeal. Is this normal appellate practice? What exactly is the legal effect of an interim order like this compared to the eventual merits opinion? I'm also not sure why the court says the government's July 17 emergency motion is "denied as moot" after changing the stay structure anyway.

questions.title: Why does 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) seem to let the President suspend refugee entry despite the Refugee Act's detailed statutory scheme?
questions.question_body: The panel says the government is likely to win on the challenge to the executive order because under Trump v. Hawaii the only prerequisite in § 1182(f) is that the President find entry would be detrimental to U.S. interests. But the Refugee Act of 1980 seems to create an ongoing framework for refugee admissions. How do courts decide whether the President's broad § 1182(f) power overrides, supplements, or is limited by the more specific refugee statutes? I feel like there should be some argument that a later, more specific statute cabins the general suspension power.

questions.title: What is the legal difference between suspending refugee 'entry' and cutting off services for refugees already admitted?
questions.question_body: One thing I can't reconcile is that the panel seems very deferential to the President on stopping future refugee admissions, but at the same time says the government is probably not going to win on at least one APA claim involving services for refugees already in the U.S. Is the key distinction that § 1182(f) only concerns entry of aliens from abroad, while domestic resettlement obligations arise from a different statute altogether? If so, why did the district court initially treat the funding suspension as tied closely enough to the executive order to enjoin it broadly?

questions.title: Did the earlier carveout for 'conditionally approved' refugees create any rights, and why was it effectively withdrawn here?
questions.question_body: Earlier in the case, the motions panel had denied a stay as to individuals who were conditionally approved for refugee status before January 20, 2025, and later clarified that carveout. In this new order, though, the court stays the district court's injunctions almost entirely and only preserves relief related to reception-and-placement services for refugees already admitted to the United States. Why wasn't the earlier carveout preserved? Does a prior stay ruling on likelihood of success have any law-of-the-case effect, or can the merits panel revisit it freely?

questions.title: Does 8 U.S.C. § 1522 impose a mandatory duty to provide refugee resettlement services, or merely authorize the Executive to do so?
questions.question_body: The majority and Judge Lee seem to read § 1522 in very different ways. The panel points to language like "shall" and specific subsections requiring the government to provide certain services, especially for unaccompanied minors and recent refugees. Judge Lee says the section's title and the repeated use of "authorized" in subsections (b)-(e) show that the statute is basically permissive, with subsection (a) just supplying conditions if the Executive chooses to fund programs. How would a court ordinarily resolve this kind of textual conflict between 'authorized' and 'shall'? Is the majority reading § 1522 as a mandatory spending statute, or only as a mandatory program-administration statute once appropriated funds exist?

questions.title: What does 'to the extent of available appropriations' actually mean for enforceability under the APA?
questions.question_body: The panel notes that Congress appropriated billions for migration and refugee assistance, though some amount was later rescinded. It then relies on § 1522's requirement that services be provided "to the extent of available appropriations." Does that phrase mean courts can review whether the agency is unlawfully withholding action once Congress has appropriated enough money, or does it still leave the Executive broad discretion about whether and how to spend those funds? I'm trying to understand whether this is really an APA 'unlawfully withheld' issue, an appropriations issue, or both.

questions.title: Can a court order the government to reinstate terminated cooperative agreements with specific nonprofits, rather than just requiring statutory compliance?
questions.question_body: The panel directs the government to "reinstate such cooperative agreements necessary" to provide the required services, including the usual services under the prior agreements. That seems like a very specific remedial order. Under the APA, I thought courts usually set aside agency action or compel action required by law, but not necessarily force the government to contract with particular private parties. What is the source of authority for this kind of remedy? Could the government comply by creating a different mechanism for delivering the services, or does the order really lock it into the old cooperative-agreement model?
